lines.t: Oh! Hi! You caught me reading.
I'm Specs.
I'm a stick figure, I wear glasses, and I collect questions.
This is my Question Jar.
People drop in the things they wonder about, and I go and find the answers.
Today, every answer is going to sound completely made up.
But I promise, every single one is true.
Ready? Let's pull out the first one.
Why is the sky blue?
Ooh, good one. Let's take a closer look.
Sunlight looks white, but it's actually every colour mixed together.
Red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet, all travelling as one.
To reach your eyes, that light has to crash through the air.
And air is packed with tiny molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen.
Here's the trick. Those molecules bounce blue light around much more than red light.
Red light has long, lazy waves. It mostly slips straight past.
Blue light has short, choppy waves, and it gets knocked all over the sky.
So wherever you look up, blue light is coming at you from every direction.
That's why the whole sky glows blue!
Scientists call it Rayleigh scattering.
But wait. Violet waves are even shorter. So why isn't the sky purple?
The Sun sends us less violet, and our eyes just aren't very good at seeing it.
And at sunset, sunlight has to travel through much more air to reach you.
Most of the blue gets scattered away on the journey, leaving the reds and oranges.
So the sky isn't painted blue. It's sunlight, bouncing around.
Next question! Is it true that octopuses have three hearts?
Yes! Three hearts. I only have one, and honestly, I'm a little jealous.
Two small hearts pump blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen.
The big third heart pumps that blood around the rest of the body.
And here's the weird part. When an octopus swims, that big heart stops beating.
Swimming is exhausting! That's why octopuses would usually rather crawl.
Oh, and their blood is blue.
Our blood uses iron to carry oxygen, and that makes it red.
Octopus blood uses copper instead, and that turns it blue.
Plus, most of an octopus's brain cells aren't in its head. They're in its arms!
Each arm can touch, taste, and make little decisions all by itself.
Three hearts, blue blood, and thinking arms. Basically an alien. But real.
Ooh, this one's a classic. Is a banana a berry?
To a botanist, a berry is a fruit that grows from one flower with a single ovary.
And its seeds are tucked inside the soft, squishy part.
Bananas fit perfectly. See those tiny dark specks in the middle?
Those are seeds that never grew up.
So yes. A banana is a berry!
And so are grapes, tomatoes, kiwis, and even eggplants.
But strawberries? Not berries at all.
A strawberry wears its seeds on the outside.
And each of those little seeds is actually its own tiny fruit.
Raspberries aren't true berries either.
So the berry aisle is lying to you. The banana aisle is not.
Next! Does honey really never go bad?
Archaeologists exploring ancient Egyptian tombs found jars of honey thousands of years old.
And it still hadn't spoiled!
So how does honey pull that off? Three tricks.
Trick one. Honey is mostly sugar, with very little water.
Any germ that lands in it gets the water sucked right out of it. It shrivels up and gives up.
Trick two. Honey is acidic, about as acidic as orange juice. Germs hate that.
Trick three. Bees add a special enzyme.
When honey gets a tiny bit wet, it makes a little hydrogen peroxide. Germ zapper!
Just keep the lid on. If honey soaks up too much water, it can start to ferment.
And if your honey turns cloudy and crunchy, it hasn't gone bad. It's just crystals.
Warm it up gently, and it melts right back.
Here's one about you. Are you taller in the morning?
You are! By about a centimetre. Sometimes more.
Your spine is a stack of bones, with squishy cushions in between, called discs.
All day long, gravity squashes you down.
Walking, sitting, standing. Your discs get squeezed and lose a little water.
Then at night, you lie down flat. The pressure's off.
And your discs soak water back up, like little sponges.
So you wake up a tiny bit taller, and shrink back down by dinner.
Astronauts take this to the extreme.
With no gravity squashing them in space, they can grow up to three percent taller!
Me? I'm a stick figure. I'm exactly as tall as whoever draws me.
Last question in the jar. Is a day on Venus really longer than its year?
We need space for this one.
A day is how long a planet takes to spin around once.
A year is how long it takes to travel all the way around the Sun.
Earth spins once a day, and circles the Sun in three hundred and sixty five days.
Venus spins incredibly slowly. One turn takes two hundred and forty three Earth days.
But it zips around the Sun in just two hundred and twenty five.
So yes! Venus finishes a whole year before it finishes a single spin.
It even spins backwards compared to Earth, so on Venus, the Sun rises in the west.
Just don't visit. The surface is hot enough to melt lead.
And that's the whole jar! Empty.
The sky is scattered sunlight. Octopuses have three hearts. Bananas are berries.
Honey lasts for thousands of years, you're taller in the morning, and a day on Venus outlasts its year.
Wait. There's one more note.
It says: What will you wonder about next?
Drop it in the jar. I'll see you next time!
